The Classifying Topos of Groups: a Case Study

A classifying topos is to a theory what a polynomial ring is to a system of unknowns: a universe containing a generic model, from which every model anywhere is obtained by substitution. This note defines the terms and then works out what all of this means, concretely, for the theory of groups. The answer is that the classifying topos is the category of functors from finitely presented groups to sets, the generic group is the forgetful functor, and “substitution” is evaluation.

By a topos we always mean a Grothendieck topos.1 The examples to keep in mind are Set\SetSet, the functor categories [C,Set][\C,\Set][C,Set] for a small category C\CC, and the category Sh(X)\Sh(X)Sh(X) of sheaves of sets on a topological space XXX. All we use about a topos E\EEE is that it has finite limits and all small colimits.

1Geometric theories

The signature of a theory consists of sorts, function symbols, and relation symbols. A sort is a name for one kind of element that the theory talks about; as in xxx is this sort of thing. A model has one underlying set for each sort, each variable ranges over a single sort, and each function symbol and relation symbol specifies the sorts of its arguments, a function symbol also specifying the sort of its value. For example, a signature for a group acting on a set has two sorts, one for group elements and one for points, and the action is a function symbol taking a group element and a point to a point. The signature of groups has one sort, a binary function symbol ⋅\cdot⋅, a unary function symbol (−)−1(-)\inv(−)−1, and a constant eee; it has no relation symbols.

Definition 1.1

A geometric formula over a signature is one built from atomic formulas (equations between terms, and relation symbols applied to terms) using

  • finite conjunctions φ∧ψ\varphi\wedge\psiφ∧ψ, including the empty conjunction ⊤\top⊤;
  • arbitrary set-indexed disjunctions ⋁i∈Iφi\bigvee_{i\in I}\varphi_i⋁i∈I​φi​, including the empty disjunction ⊥\bot⊥, as long as the whole formula has only finitely many free variables;
  • existential quantification ∃y φ\exists y\,\varphi∃yφ.

A geometric sequent is an expression φ⊢x‾ψ\varphi\vdash_{\underline{x}}\psiφ⊢x​​ψ, where φ\varphiφ and ψ\psiψ are geometric formulas whose free variables are among the finite list x‾\underline{x}x​. It is read as “for all x‾\underline{x}x​, if φ\varphiφ then ψ\psiψ.” A geometric theory T\TTT is a set of geometric sequents, its axioms.

Negation, implication, and universal quantification are not allowed inside a geometric formula. Implication and universal quantification enter only through the sequent: in first-order notation the sequent φ⊢x‾ψ\varphi\vdash_{\underline{x}}\psiφ⊢x​​ψ is the sentence ∀x‾ (φ→ψ)\forall\underline{x}\,(\varphi\rightarrow\psi)∀x​(φ→ψ). Each axiom therefore uses exactly one implication, with the universal quantifiers over x‾\underline{x}x​ in front of the implication, and neither →\rightarrow→ nor ∀\forall∀ occurs inside φ\varphiφ or ψ\psiψ.

Example 1.2 (Groups)

The theory of groups, which we call G\GGG, has the axioms ⊤⊢x,y,z(x⋅y)⋅z=x⋅(y⋅z),⊤⊢xx⋅e=x∧e⋅x=x,⊤⊢xx⋅x−1=e∧x−1⋅x=e. \top\vdash_{x,y,z}(x\cdot y)\cdot z=x\cdot(y\cdot z),\qquad \top\vdash_{x}x\cdot e=x\wedge e\cdot x=x,\qquad \top\vdash_{x}x\cdot x\inv=e\wedge x\inv\cdot x=e. ⊤⊢x,y,z​(x⋅y)⋅z=x⋅(y⋅z),⊤⊢x​x⋅e=x∧e⋅x=x,⊤⊢x​x⋅x−1=e∧x−1⋅x=e. Each axiom is an equation with ⊤\top⊤ on the left. A theory of this shape is called algebraic, and it is the simplest kind of geometric theory: it uses neither ⋁\bigvee⋁ nor ∃\exists∃.

Example 1.3 (Using the other connectives)

Adding axioms to G\GGG gives further geometric theories.

  • Abelian groups: add ⊤⊢x,yx⋅y=y⋅x\top\vdash_{x,y}x\cdot y=y\cdot x⊤⊢x,y​x⋅y=y⋅x.
  • Torsion-free groups: add xn=e⊢xx=ex^n=e\vdash_x x=exn=e⊢x​x=e for each n≥1n\ge1n≥1.
  • Divisible groups: add ⊤⊢x∃y (yn=x)\top\vdash_x\exists y\,(y^n=x)⊤⊢x​∃y(yn=x) for each n≥1n\ge1n≥1.
  • Torsion groups: add ⊤⊢x⋁n≥1xn=e\top\vdash_x\bigvee_{n\ge1}x^n=e⊤⊢x​⋁n≥1​xn=e.

The last one is not expressible in ordinary first-order logic, where disjunctions are finite. In the other direction, the first-order statement that a group has trivial center, ∀x ((∀y,  x⋅y=y⋅x)→x=e), \forall x\,\bigl((\forall y,\;x\cdot y=y\cdot x)\rightarrow x=e\bigr), ∀x((∀y,x⋅y=y⋅x)→x=e), is not a geometric sequent, because of the ∀y\forall y∀y on the left of the implication. No geometric theory has the centerless groups as its models; see the remark after Proposition 9.1.

The reason for this particular fragment of logic is that ∧\wedge∧ is interpreted by finite limits, and ⋁\bigvee⋁ and ∃\exists∃ by colimits. Finite limits and arbitrary colimits are exactly what the geometric morphisms between toposes preserve (Definition 3.1), so geometric sequents are the statements whose truth can be transported from one topos to another.

2Models in a topos

A group is a set with operations satisfying equations. The definition makes sense with “set” replaced by “object of E\EEE” as soon as the equations are written as commuting diagrams.

Definition 2.1

A group object in a topos E\EEE, or a model of G\GGG in E\EEE, is an object HHH of E\EEE with morphisms m:H×H→H,i:H→H,e:1→H, m:H\times H\to H,\qquad i:H\to H,\qquad e:1\to H, m:H×H→H,i:H→H,e:1→H, where 111 is the terminal object, such that the diagrams expressing associativity, the unit laws, and the inverse laws commute. For example, associativity says that the two morphisms m∘(m×id)m\circ(m\times\mathrm{id})m∘(m×id) and m∘(id×m)m\circ(\mathrm{id}\times m)m∘(id×m) from H×H×HH\times H\times HH×H×H to HHH are equal. Equivalently, the following square commutes.

A homomorphism of group objects is a morphism H→H′H\to H'H→H′ of E\EEE commuting with mmm, iii, and eee. We write Grp(E)\Grp(\EE)Grp(E) for the category of group objects in E\EEE.

An equivalent and often more convenient description uses generalized elements. For an object ZZZ of E\EEE, a ZZZ-element of HHH is a morphism Z→HZ\to HZ→H. Then HHH is a group object exactly when each set E(Z,H)\EE(Z,H)E(Z,H) of ZZZ-elements is a group, in such a way that composition with any Z′→ZZ'\to ZZ′→Z is a group homomorphism E(Z,H)→E(Z′,H)\EE(Z,H)\to\EE(Z',H)E(Z,H)→E(Z′,H). This is the Yoneda lemma applied to mmm, iii and eee.2

For a general geometric theory T\TTT, a model in E\EEE assigns an object to each sort, a morphism to each function symbol, and a subobject to each relation symbol. A formula φ\varphiφ with free variables x‾\underline{x}x​ of sorts interpreted by A1,…,AnA_1,\dots,A_nA1​,…,An​ then defines a subobject [ ⁣[φ] ⁣]⊆A1×⋯×An[\![\varphi]\!]\subseteq A_1\times\dots\times A_n[[φ]]⊆A1​×⋯×An​, “the set of x‾\underline{x}x​ satisfying φ\varphiφ”: equations are interpreted by equalizers, ∧\wedge∧ by intersection, ⋁\bigvee⋁ by union, and ∃\exists∃ by image under a projection. The structure is a model if [ ⁣[φ] ⁣]⊆[ ⁣[ψ] ⁣][\![\varphi]\!]\subseteq[\![\psi]\!][[φ]]⊆[[ψ]] for every axiom φ⊢x‾ψ\varphi\vdash_{\underline{x}}\psiφ⊢x​​ψ. For an algebraic theory such as G\GGG this reduces to commuting diagrams as in Definition 2.1.

Example 2.2 (Sets)

A group object in Set\SetSet is a group.

Example 2.3 (Sheaves)

A group object in Sh(X)\Sh(X)Sh(X) is a sheaf of groups on XXX: a sheaf HHH with a group structure on each H(V)H(V)H(V), for V⊆XV\subseteq XV⊆X open, such that the restriction maps are homomorphisms. This is the generalized-element description, restricted to the ZZZ that are open subsets of XXX. Intuitively, a group in Sh(X)\Sh(X)Sh(X) is a group that varies continuously over XXX.

For a concrete example, let AAA be a topological group and let CAC_ACA​ be the sheaf on XXX whose sections over an open subset V⊆XV\subseteq XV⊆X are the continuous AAA-valued functions on VVV, CA(V)={continuous maps V→A}, C_A(V)=\{\text{continuous maps }V\to A\}, CA​(V)={continuous maps V→A}, with pointwise multiplication.

Sheaves also show what is new about the logic. Take A=C×A=\CC^\timesA=C× and consider the geometric sequent ⊤⊢x∃y (y2=x)\top\vdash_x\exists y\,(y^2=x)⊤⊢x​∃y(y2=x) which asserts that the group is 222-divisible. Geometrically, the formula ∃y (y2=x)\exists y\,(y^2=x)∃y(y2=x) is interpreted as describing the xxx which form the image of the squaring map CC×→CC×C_{\CC^\times}\to C_{\CC^\times}CC×​→CC×​, and images in Sh(X)\Sh(X)Sh(X) are computed locally. A continuous function V→C×V\to\CC^\timesV→C× has a continuous square root in a neighborhood of each point, so the image is everything and the sequent holds: the group object CC×C_{\CC^\times}CC×​ is 222-divisible. But on X=C×X=\CC^\timesX=C× the function zzz has no global square root, so the group CC×(X)C_{\CC^\times}(X)CC×​(X) of global sections is not 222-divisible. The local reading of ∃\exists∃ is not special to Sh(X)\Sh(X)Sh(X): in every topos E\EEE, “there exists” means “there exists locally,” where “locally” means “after pulling back along an epimorphism.”

Example 2.4 (Functor categories)

A group object in [C,Set][\C,\Set][C,Set] is a functor C→Grp\C\to\GrpC→Grp. To see why, let H:C→SetH:\C\to\SetH:C→Set be a group object, with natural transformations m:H×H→Hm:H\times H\to Hm:H×H→H, i:H→Hi:H\to Hi:H→H and e:1→He:1\to He:1→H. Limits in [C,Set][\C,\Set][C,Set] are computed pointwise, which for the finite products in Definition 2.1 means that (H×H)(c)=H(c)×H(c)(H\times H)(c)=H(c)\times H(c)(H×H)(c)=H(c)×H(c) and that 1(c)1(c)1(c) is a single point for every object ccc of C\CC. The components of mmm, iii and eee at ccc are therefore maps mc:H(c)×H(c)→H(c)m_c:H(c)\times H(c)\to H(c)mc​:H(c)×H(c)→H(c), ic:H(c)→H(c)i_c:H(c)\to H(c)ic​:H(c)→H(c) and ec:1→H(c)e_c:1\to H(c)ec​:1→H(c), that is, a multiplication, an inversion and a distinguished element on the set H(c)H(c)H(c). Two natural transformations are equal exactly when their components at every ccc are equal, so the diagrams of Definition 2.1 commute in [C,Set][\C,\Set][C,Set] exactly when the corresponding diagrams of sets commute for every ccc, which says that each H(c)H(c)H(c) is a group. For an arrow u:c→c′u:c\to c'u:c→c′ of C\CC, the product functor H×HH\times HH×H sends uuu to H(u)×H(u)H(u)\times H(u)H(u)×H(u), so naturality of mmm says that H(u)(mc(a,b))=mc′(H(u)(a),H(u)(b))H(u)(m_c(a,b))=m_{c'}(H(u)(a),H(u)(b))H(u)(mc​(a,b))=mc′​(H(u)(a),H(u)(b)) for all a,b∈H(c)a,b\in H(c)a,b∈H(c), which is the statement that H(u):H(c)→H(c′)H(u):H(c)\to H(c')H(u):H(c)→H(c′) is a group homomorphism. Conversely, for a functor C→Grp\C\to\GrpC→Grp, the group operations on the groups H(c)H(c)H(c) are the components of natural transformations mmm, iii and eee that make the underlying functor H:C→SetH:\C\to\SetH:C→Set a group object. If C\CC is the category ∙→∙\bullet\to\bullet∙→∙ with two objects and one non-identity arrow, a group object is a group homomorphism G0→G1G_0\to G_1G0​→G1​. 3The classifying topos

Definition 3.1

A geometric morphism f:E→Ff:\EE\to\mathcal{F}f:E→F between toposes is a pair of adjoint functors f∗:F→E,f∗:E→F,f∗⊣f∗, f^*:\mathcal{F}\to\EE,\qquad f_*:\EE\to\mathcal{F},\qquad f^*\dashv f_*, f∗:F→E,f∗​:E→F,f∗⊣f∗​, such that the left adjoint f∗f^*f∗ preserves finite limits. We call f∗f^*f∗ the inverse image and f∗f_*f∗​ the direct image. A morphism f→gf\to gf→g of geometric morphisms is a natural transformation f∗→g∗f^*\to g^*f∗→g∗. We write Geom(E,F)\Geom(\EE,\mathcal{F})Geom(E,F) for the resulting category.

The model for this definition is a continuous map f:X→Yf:X\to Yf:X→Y, which induces a geometric morphism Sh(X)→Sh(Y)\Sh(X)\to\Sh(Y)Sh(X)→Sh(Y) whose inverse image is pullback of sheaves. Note the directions: the geometric morphism points the way the map of spaces does, and the inverse image functor, which carries most of the information, points the other way. A geometric morphism Set→E\Set\to\EESet→E is called a point of E\EEE, since Set=Sh(pt)\Set=\Sh(\mathrm{pt})Set=Sh(pt).

Being a left adjoint, f∗f^*f∗ preserves all colimits, and by assumption it preserves finite limits. So f∗f^*f∗ preserves everything used to interpret geometric logic. In particular f∗f^*f∗ preserves finite products, so if HHH is a group object in F\mathcal{F}F then f∗Hf^*Hf∗H is a group object in E\EEE, with multiplication f∗(m)f^*(m)f∗(m). The same holds for models of any geometric theory T\TTT: there is a functor f∗:ModT(F)→ModT(E)f^*:\Mod_\TT(\mathcal{F})\to\Mod_\TT(\EE)f∗:ModT​(F)→ModT​(E).

Definition 3.2

A classifying topos for a geometric theory T\TTT is a topos Set[T]\Set[\TT]Set[T] together with a model UUU of T\TTT in Set[T]\Set[\TT]Set[T], the universal model, such that for every topos E\EEE the functor Geom(E,Set[T])⟶ModT(E),f⟼f∗U, \Geom(\EE,\Set[\TT])\longrightarrow\Mod_\TT(\EE),\qquad f\longmapsto f^*U, Geom(E,Set[T])⟶ModT​(E),f⟼f∗U, is an equivalence of categories.

In words: every model MMM of T\TTT in every topos E\EEE is the pullback f∗Uf^*Uf∗U of the universal model along a geometric morphism f:E→Set[T]f:\EE\to\Set[\TT]f:E→Set[T], and fff is unique up to unique isomorphism. Homomorphisms of models correspond to natural transformations of inverse image functors. Taking E=Set\EE=\SetE=Set, the points of Set[T]\Set[\TT]Set[T] are the ordinary set-based models of T\TTT.

Theorem 3.3

Every geometric theory has a classifying topos, unique up to equivalence [1, Chapter X], [2, Part D].

Two analogies are useful. The first is the classifying space BABABA of a topological group AAA: principal AAA-bundles on a space XXX are the pullbacks of the universal bundle along maps X→BAX\to BAX→BA. The second is algebraic. The polynomial ring Z[x]\ZZ[x]Z[x] with its element xxx has the property that for every commutative ring RRR, HomRing(Z[x],R)⟶R,φ⟼φ(x), \Hom_{\mathrm{Ring}}(\ZZ[x],R)\longrightarrow R,\qquad \varphi\longmapsto\varphi(x), HomRing​(Z[x],R)⟶R,φ⟼φ(x), is a bijection: Z[x]\ZZ[x]Z[x] is the free ring on one element, and xxx is the generic element. The notation Set[T]\Set[\TT]Set[T] is chosen to suggest this. If we think of a topos algebraically, with its inverse image functors f∗f^*f∗ playing the role of ring homomorphisms, then Set[T]\Set[\TT]Set[T] is the topos freely generated by a model of T\TTT, and UUU is the generic model, playing the role of the variable xxx. We return to this analogy in Section 11, where it becomes surprisingly literal.

4The classifying topos of groups

Let FPGrp\FPFPGrp be the category of finitely presented groups and all homomorphisms between them. A group is finitely presented if it is isomorphic to ⟨x1,…,xn∣r1,…,rm⟩ \langle x_1,\dots,x_n\mid r_1,\dots,r_m\rangle ⟨x1​,…,xn​∣r1​,…,rm​⟩ for finitely many generators and finitely many relators rjr_jrj​, which are words in the xi±1x_i^{\pm1}xi±1​.3 There are only countably many finite presentations, so FPGrp\FPFPGrp is equivalent to a small category, and we do not distinguish it from one.4

Theorem 4.1

The classifying topos of the theory of groups is the category of covariant functors from finitely presented groups to sets, Set[G]=[FPGrp,Set], \Set[\GG]=[\FP,\Set], Set[G]=[FPGrp,Set], and the universal model is the forgetful functor U:FPGrp→SetU:\FP\to\SetU:FPGrp→Set, which sends a group to its underlying set.

The theorem holds, with the same proof, for any algebraic theory in place of groups; Mac Lane and Moerdijk treat the case of rings [1, Chapter VIII]. The rest of this note is not so much a proof as an unpacking. For a group object HHH in a topos E\EEE we will write down the geometric morphism fH:E→[FPGrp,Set]f_H:\EE\to[\FP,\Set]fH​:E→[FPGrp,Set] with fH∗U≅Hf_H^*U\cong HfH∗​U≅H, in increasing generality, and see why it is the only one. The one step we quote without proof is the exactness statement in Theorem 11.2.

An object FFF of [FPGrp,Set][\FP,\Set][FPGrp,Set] is a set F(K)F(K)F(K) for each finitely presented group KKK, and a map F(φ):F(K)→F(L)F(\varphi):F(K)\to F(L)F(φ):F(K)→F(L) for each homomorphism φ:K→L\varphi:K\to Lφ:K→L. Some examples, to have something to compute with:

  • U(K)=KU(K)=KU(K)=K, the underlying set.
  • K↦K×KK\mapsto K\times KK↦K×K, or K↦KnK\mapsto K^nK↦Kn.
  • K↦{k∈K:kn=e}K\mapsto\{k\in K:k^n=e\}K↦{k∈K:kn=e}, the nnn-torsion elements.
  • K↦{(k,l)∈K2:kl=lk}K\mapsto\{(k,l)\in K^2:kl=lk\}K↦{(k,l)∈K2:kl=lk}, the commuting pairs.
  • K↦K/conjugationK\mapsto K/\mathrm{conjugation}K↦K/conjugation, the set of conjugacy classes.
  • K↦{k∈K:k has finite order}K\mapsto\{k\in K:k\text{ has finite order}\}K↦{k∈K:k has finite order}, the torsion elements.
  • K↦SK\mapsto SK↦S, a constant functor.

A non-example is K↦Z(K)K\mapsto Z(K)K↦Z(K), the center: a homomorphism does not map the center into the center. The objects of Set[G]\Set[\GG]Set[G] are the sets that can be built naturally out of a group.

5Why finitely presented groups?

Why not the category of functors from all groups to sets? One issue is size: Grp\GrpGrp is not a small category, and [Grp,Set][\Grp,\Set][Grp,Set] is not a topos. The better answer is that finite presentations are exactly as much as geometric logic can see.

By (4.1), a finitely presented group KKK is the same thing as a finite conjunction of equations in finitely many variables, (r1(x‾)=e)∧⋯∧(rm(x‾)=e), (r_1(\underline{x})=e)\wedge\dots\wedge (r_m(\underline{x})=e), (r1​(x​)=e)∧⋯∧(rm​(x​)=e), which is a geometric formula, and the monomial XKX^KXK is its interpretation in the generic group. In terms of limits, XKX^KXK is the equalizer of two maps Xn⇉XmX^n\rightrightarrows X^mXn⇉Xm, namely x‾↦(rj(x‾))j\underline{x}\mapsto(r_j(\underline{x}))_jx​↦(rj​(x​))j​ and the constant map eee. This is a finite limit built from XXX, so an inverse image functor f∗f^*f∗ must preserve it, and the value of f∗f^*f∗ on XKX^KXK is forced by the value of f∗f^*f∗ on XXX. This is the mechanism behind the universal property.

For an infinitely presented group KKK, the functor XKX^KXK is an infinite limit of copies of XXX, or the interpretation of an infinite conjunction. Inverse image functors need not preserve it, so if such functors were objects of our topos, knowing f∗Xf^*Xf∗X would not determine f∗f^*f∗. The topos would be too big to be freely generated by the generic group.

Nothing is lost by the restriction, for a different reason: every group is a filtered colimit5 of finitely presented groups, and we will see in Section 9 that every functor FFF on FPGrp\FPFPGrp extends canonically to all groups. Under this extension [FPGrp,Set][\FP,\Set][FPGrp,Set] is equivalent to the category of functors Grp→Set\Grp\to\SetGrp→Set that preserve filtered colimits. The functors XK:Grp→SetX^K:\Grp\to\SetXK:Grp→Set that preserve filtered colimits are exactly those with KKK finitely presented; this is the categorical meaning of finite presentation.

Finally, note that finite generation would not be enough. For XKX^KXK to be a finite limit we need finitely many relations as well as finitely many generators.

6The universal model

The universal model is XXX, the forgetful functor. To make it a group object in [FPGrp,Set][\FP,\Set][FPGrp,Set] we need natural transformations m:X×X→X,i:X→X,e:1→X. m:X\times X\to X,\qquad i:X\to X,\qquad e:1\to X. m:X×X→X,i:X→X,e:1→X. Products in a functor category are pointwise, so (X×X)(K)=K×K(X\times X)(K)=K\times K(X×X)(K)=K×K, and we define each operation componentwise: mK:K×K→Kis the multiplication of K, m_K:K\times K\to K\quad\text{is the multiplication of }K, mK​:K×K→Kis the multiplication of K, and similarly iKi_KiK​ is inversion in KKK and eKe_KeK​ is the identity element of KKK. Naturality of mmm says that for every homomorphism φ:K→L\varphi:K\to Lφ:K→L, φ(k1k2)=φ(k1)φ(k2), \varphi(k_1k_2)=\varphi(k_1)\varphi(k_2), φ(k1​k2​)=φ(k1​)φ(k2​), which is the statement that φ\varphiφ is a homomorphism. The group axioms are equations between natural transformations, and they hold because they hold in each component.

So the generic group is something like the tuple X=(K)K∈FPGrp X=(K)_{K\in\FP} X=(K)K∈FPGrp​ of all finitely presented groups at once, with all operations performed componentwise: a superposition of every group. The tuple is not the same as the product group ∏KK\prod_KK∏K​K, because XXX is a functor and not only a family of groups: XXX also records, for every homomorphism φ:K→L\varphi:K\to Lφ:K→L, the map φ\varphiφ from the KKKth component to the LLLth component. Maps into and out of XXX are natural transformations, so they must commute with the maps φ\varphiφ. For example, an element of the product ∏KK\prod_KK∏K​K is an arbitrary choice of one element kK∈Kk_K\in KkK​∈K for each KKK, whereas an element of XXX, meaning a natural transformation 1→X1\to X1→X, is such a choice subject to the condition φ(kK)=kL\varphi(k_K)=k_Lφ(kK​)=kL​ for every homomorphism φ:K→L\varphi:K\to Lφ:K→L.

Remark (Elements of the generic group)

A global element of XXX is a natural transformation 1→X1\to X1→X: a choice of an element in every finitely presented group, compatible with all homomorphisms. The only such choice is the identity element, since 1=X01=X^01=X0, where 0={e}0=\{e\}0={e} is the trivial group, and by (4.2) Nat(X0,X)=X(0)\Nat(X^0,X)=X(0)Nat(X0,X)=X(0) has one element. The generic group has only one global element, despite “containing” every group.

It has many generalized elements. By (4.2), Nat(XK,X)=K\Nat(X^K,X)=KNat(XK,X)=K, which is to say that an element of the generic group defined on the solution set of the equations of KKK is an element of KKK. For K=FnK=F_nK=Fn​ this says that the natural operations Gn→GG^n\to GGn→G defined on all groups are the words in nnn letters, which is a good way to remember why free groups consist of words. The multiplication m:X2→Xm:X^2\to Xm:X2→X is the word x1x2∈F2x_1x_2\in F_2x1​x2​∈F2​.

Limits and colimits in [FPGrp,Set][\FP,\Set][FPGrp,Set] are computed componentwise, and so is the interpretation of geometric formulas. So a geometric sequent holds in XXX exactly when it holds in every finitely presented group. The generic group is not abelian, since some groups are not, and not torsion-free; it has exactly the geometric properties shared by all groups. This is what makes it universal: it has no special properties to obstruct mapping it to any other group.

The generic group is not a free group, although both are universal. A free group FnF_nFn​ is an ordinary group, that is, a group object in Set\SetSet, whereas XXX is a group object in [FPGrp,Set][\FP,\Set][FPGrp,Set], which by Example 2.4 is a functor FPGrp→Grp\FP\to\GrpFPGrp→Grp, namely the inclusion. A free group and the generic group are also universal in different senses. A homomorphism Fn→HF_n\to HFn​→H is a choice of nnn elements of HHH, so FnF_nFn​ is universal among groups equipped with nnn chosen elements, and a homomorphism from FnF_nFn​ reaches only the subgroup of HHH generated by those nnn elements. The generic group reaches HHH by substitution instead of by a homomorphism: the inverse image functor fH∗f_H^*fH∗​ constructed in the sections that follow carries XXX to HHH itself, with nothing chosen and nothing lost. No free group could be substituted in the same way, whether the free group has finitely or infinitely many generators, because every free group is torsion-free, and torsion-freeness is a geometric property (Example 1.3) that inverse image functors preserve and that many groups lack. Free groups do appear inside the generic group, one for each number of generators: X(Fn)=FnX(F_n)=F_nX(Fn​)=Fn​, and by (4.2) the elements of XXX defined on XnX^nXn form the group Nat(Xn,X)=Fn\Nat(X^n,X)=F_nNat(Xn,X)=Fn​. The freeness in the universal property belongs to the topos and not to the group: [FPGrp,Set][\FP,\Set][FPGrp,Set] is the free topos on one group in the way that Z[x]\ZZ[x]Z[x] is the free ring, and F1F_1F1​ the free group, on one element xxx. The generic group XXX corresponds to the element xxx, not to Z[x]\ZZ[x]Z[x] or F1F_1F1​.

So an element of F(G)F(G)F(G) is an element of some F(Gn)F(G_n)F(Gn​), and two of them are equal if they agree in some later F(Gn′)F(G_{n'})F(Gn′​). The points fGf_GfG​ for GGG not finitely presented are not essential. The functor fG∗f_G^*fG∗​ preserves finite limits but not infinite ones, since filtered colimits do not commute with infinite products, and so it has no left adjoint.

Polynomials in a group variable

Is [FPGrp,Set][\FP,\Set][FPGrp,Set] something like a ring of polynomials, or power series, in the monomials XKX^KXK? And is density just the statement that the monomials generate, so that a homomorphism is determined by its values on them? Yes, and the analogy can be pushed quite far. The analogy between toposes and commutative rings, with colimits as sums and finite limits as products, is developed by Anel and Joyal [3]. There are three places where the dictionary should be read with care.

Polynomials or power series? The coefficients are sets, and sets can be added up infinitely often with no question of convergence, so the sums are allowed to be infinite. The functor ∑n≥0Xn=∑n≥0XFn, \sum_{n\ge0}X^n=\sum_{n\ge0}X^{F_n}, n≥0∑​Xn=n≥0∑​XFn​, which sends a group to the set of finite lists of its elements, is an object of [FPGrp,Set][\FP,\Set][FPGrp,Set], and it is the power series 1/(1−X)1/(1-X)1/(1−X). In this respect the objects are power series. But each monomial is finite, in the sense that KKK is finitely presented, and Section 5 explains that this finiteness is essential. So the truth is in between: possibly infinite sums of finite monomials, and the distinction between polynomials and power series does not arise.

Sums with gluing. A colimit is more than a sum. The coend (11.1) is a quotient of the sum ∐KF(K)×XK\coprod_KF(K)\times X^K∐K​F(K)×XK, and the quotient matters. The functor of torsion elements is the union Xtors=⋃n≥1XZ/n, X_{\mathrm{tors}}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}X^{\ZZ/n}, Xtors​=n≥1⋃​XZ/n, a colimit over the divisibility order in which XZ/2X^{\ZZ/2}XZ/2 is glued into XZ/4X^{\ZZ/4}XZ/4, and not the disjoint union. The functor of conjugacy classes in Example 11.3 is a quotient of the single monomial XXX. The monomials are not linearly independent, so to speak: they are related by the maps Xφ:XL→XKX^\varphi:X^L\to X^KXφ:XL→XK, and the coend identifies along all of them. A closer analogy than the polynomial ring is a module given by generators and relations, or a tensor product: (11.1) is often written F⊗FPGrpX(−)F\otimes_{\FP}X^{(-)}F⊗FPGrp​X(−).

The variable is a group. For a polynomial ring the monomials are the powers of xxx. Here the powers Xn=XFnX^n=X^{F_n}Xn=XFn​ are only some of the monomials, and the rest are the subobjects XK⊆XnX^K\subseteq X^nXK⊆Xn cut out by equations. These exist because XXX is not a bare variable: it carries a group structure, and finite limits include equalizers as well as products. The bare variable has its own classifying topos, the object classifier [FinSet,Set][\mathbf{FinSet},\Set][FinSet,Set], whose monomials are exactly the powers XnX^nXn of the inclusion functor XXX, and which really is the polynomial ring Set[X]\Set[X]Set[X] in one variable.

12Reflections

Everything is substitution. The classifying topos is a category of expressions F(X)F(X)F(X) in a group variable XXX. A group object HHH in a topos E\EEE gives a way to evaluate these expressions, F↦F(H)F\mapsto F(H)F↦F(H), and conversely every reasonable evaluation functor comes from a unique HHH, which is recovered as the value of the expression XXX. The cases we went through differ only in how the substitution is carried out: by evaluating the functor when HHH is a finitely presented group, by a filtered colimit when HHH is any group, and by a coend in general.

The objects are geometric constructions. The objects of Set[G]\Set[\GG]Set[G] are the sets that can be constructed from a group using finite limits and arbitrary colimits: solution sets of equations, their unions and quotients. These are the constructions that make sense for a group object in any topos and are preserved by every inverse image functor. The center of a group is not such a construction, and neither is the set of all subgroups.

The theory is in the topos. The category FPGrpop\FP^{\mathrm{op}}FPGrpop is a presentation-free form of the theory of groups: its objects are the finite systems of equations, and its morphisms are the substitutions that carry solutions to solutions. The topos [FPGrp,Set][\FP,\Set][FPGrp,Set] is built from it by adjoining colimits. Two theories with equivalent classifying toposes have the same models in every topos, even if their signatures and axioms look different, so the topos is an invariant of the theory that forgets the presentation.

What changes for other theories. For an algebraic theory, the story is the same with “group” replaced throughout: rings are classified by functors from finitely presented rings to sets. Axioms that use ⋁\bigvee⋁ or ∃\exists∃ cannot be imposed by equalizers. Instead each such axiom says that a certain family of maps is jointly surjective, and one passes from all functors to the sheaves for which these families are covers. Adding axioms to a geometric theory replaces its classifying topos by a subtopos [4]. The standard example is the theory of local rings, whose classifying topos is the topos of sheaves on the Zariski site, sitting inside the classifying topos of rings [1, Chapter VIII]. It would be interesting to work out what the subtoposes of [FPGrp,Set][\FP,\Set][FPGrp,Set] are for the theories in Example 1.3.

13Further reading

  • Mac Lane and Moerdijk [1]: Chapter VII for geometric morphisms and Diaconescu's theorem, Chapter VIII for classifying toposes, including rings and local rings, and Chapter X for geometric logic and the existence theorem.
  • Johnstone [2, Part D] for the general theory, including the fragments of geometric logic and their syntactic categories.
  • Caramello [4] for classifying toposes as a tool for comparing theories.
  • Anel and Joyal [3] for the algebraic point of view on toposes used in Section 11.

A sheaf on the site is a functor F:Cop→SetF:\C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\SetF:Cop→Set such that, for every cover {Ui→U}\{U_i\to U\}{Ui​→U}, an element of F(U)F(U)F(U) is the same thing as a compatible family of elements of the sets F(Ui)F(U_i)F(Ui​). The open sets of a topological space XXX with the usual open covers form a site whose sheaves are Sh(X)\Sh(X)Sh(X), and when only the trivial families are covers every functor Cop→Set\C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\SetCop→Set is a sheaf. ↩

  4. A category is small if its objects form a set rather than a proper class, and the functor category [C,Set][\C,\Set][C,Set] is only guaranteed to be a topos when C\CC is small. Taken literally, FPGrp\FPFPGrp is not small: every set in bijection with the underlying set of a finitely presented group KKK carries a group structure isomorphic to KKK, so the finitely presented groups form a proper class. The size of FPGrp\FPFPGrp comes entirely from these isomorphic copies. A finite presentation is a finite list of generators x1,…,xnx_1,\dots,x_nx1​,…,xn​ together with a finite list of words in the xi±1x_i^{\pm1}xi±1​, so there are only countably many finite presentations, and every finitely presented group is by definition isomorphic to one of the countably many groups ⟨x1,…,xn∣r1,…,rm⟩\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\mid r_1,\dots,r_m\rangle⟨x1​,…,xn​∣r1​,…,rm​⟩. The full subcategory of FPGrp\FPFPGrp whose objects are these countably many groups is small, and the inclusion of this subcategory into FPGrp\FPFPGrp is an equivalence of categories, because the inclusion is fully faithful and every object of FPGrp\FPFPGrp is isomorphic to an object of the subcategory. Restricting a functor FPGrp→Set\FP\to\SetFPGrp→Set to the subcategory loses no information, since the value of the functor on any finitely presented group is determined up to isomorphism by its value on an isomorphic group in the subcategory. ↩
